t_korea.overview: South Korea's Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust (the AI Basic Act) has been in force since 22 January 2026 and is the country's overarching AI law. It pairs state promotion of the AI industry with a light set of trust duties enforced by the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT). Those duties are advance notice and labeling for generative and high-impact AI, six risk-management measures for high-impact AI, safety duties for frontier-compute systems, and a domestic representative for large foreign operators. The Enforcement Decree (Presidential Decree No. 36053) supplies the thresholds and procedures.
t_korea.exam: Expect EU contrasts. Korea has no prohibited practices, and its fines are capped at KRW 30 million for only three failures. Its impact assessment is best-efforts rather than mandatory, MSIT is the single regulator, and MSIT's grace period of at least a year is policy, not statute. Know the high-impact domain list, the 10^26 FLOP threshold versus the EU's 10^25, and the domestic-representative thresholds.
key_points: Promulgated 21 Jan 2025 (Act No. 20676) and in force 22 Jan 2026; the Enforcement Decree (No. 36053) sets the numbers, and MSIT enforces

High-impact AI = a listed domain (energy, water, health, medical devices, nuclear, policing biometrics, hiring and lending judgments, transport, public decisions, K-12 assessment) plus significant risk to life, safety or rights
High-impact measures: risk management plan, explanation plan, user protection, human oversight and documents kept 5 years; the impact assessment is best efforts only

Transparency: advance notice for high-impact and generative AI, labels on generative outputs (human- or machine-readable), and a clear notice for realistic synthetic media, with a softer method allowed for artistic works
Article 32 safety duties cover systems of at least 10^26 FLOPs that are state of the art and pose wide-ranging risk; results go to MSIT (the EU presumes systemic risk at 10^25)
A foreign operator meeting any threshold (KRW 1 trillion revenue, KRW 10 billion AI revenue, 1 million daily Korean users) must appoint a domestic representative

Fines of up to KRW 30 million apply only to missing notice, a missing representative or an ignored order; other breaches go to fact-finding and corrective orders, with an MSIT grace period of at least one year

term:High-Impact AI (Korea).deep_dive: This is Korea's counterpart to the EU's high-risk category, but it is defined in the statute rather than an annex. A system qualifies only if it sits in a domain listed in Art. 2(4) and could significantly affect life, safety or fundamental rights. Operators must check status in advance and may ask MSIT to confirm, with an answer due within 30 days (extendable once). High-impact status triggers advance notice, the six Art. 34 measures and a best-efforts impact assessment, but no conformity assessment or registration.
term:High-Impact AI (Korea).exam_tip: Being in a listed domain isn't enough on its own, and student assessment counts only from early childhood through secondary school.

term:AI Business Operator (Korea).deep_dive: The Act regulates 'AI business operators' of two kinds: developers that build and supply AI, and AI-using business operators that build products or services on a developer's AI. Unlike the EU's split between provider and deployer, most duties attach to whichever operator provides the product or service. The decree eases this for downstream operators. One that makes no significant functional change is deemed to have carried out the developer's risk-management, explanation and user-protection measures.
term:AI Business Operator (Korea).exam_tip: Government bodies count as AI business operators too, and the deeming rule never covers human oversight or documentation.

term:Domestic Representative (Korea AI B.deep_dive: This is Korea's version of the EU's authorized representative, but only size triggers it: a foreign operator with no Korean address must appoint one if it meets any one decree threshold. The representative files Art. 32 safety results, requests high-impact confirmations and supports the Art. 34 measures, including checking that records are current and accurate. Any violation by the representative is treated as the foreign operator's own.
term:Domestic Representative (Korea AI B.exam_tip: The thresholds are alternatives, so meeting any one is enough, and failing to appoint a representative is one of only three directly finable violations.

term:Generative AI Labeling (Korea).deep_dive: Art. 31(2) requires operators to indicate that generative AI outputs are AI-generated. The decree accepts methods humans can recognize or machine-readable ones such as watermarks, but a machine-readable mark must come with at least one text or voice notice. Art. 31(3) adds a stricter, clearly recognizable notice for realistic synthetic sound, images and video, with a less intrusive method allowed for artistic or creative works. The duties can be waived where AI use is obvious or the AI is used only internally.
term:Generative AI Labeling (Korea).exam_tip: A labeling breach isn't fined directly (MSIT investigates and orders a fix, and only an ignored order draws a fine), unlike the separate advance-notice duty in Art. 31(1), which is fined outright.

term:Korea AI Basic Act Enforcement Decr.deep_dive: The Act leaves most of its numbers and procedures to this Presidential Decree, which was issued after public consultation on the subordinate legislation during 2025. It sets the three-part test for the Art. 32 safety duties (10^26 FLOPs, state of the art, wide-ranging risk), the domestic-representative thresholds, the notice and labeling methods and their exemptions, and the 30-day high-impact confirmation process. It also fixes five-year document retention, lists what an impact assessment covers, and creates the deemed-compliance rule for AI-using operators. MSIT notices and guidelines sit below it.
term:Korea AI Basic Act Enforcement Decr.exam_tip: Korea's 10^26 FLOP figure and the KRW 1 trillion representative threshold come from the decree, not the Act.

term:Best-Efforts Impact Assessment (Kor.deep_dive: Art. 35 asks operators providing high-impact AI to try to assess its impact on fundamental rights before offering it. Skipping it brings no fine, and it cannot trigger fact-finding. The incentive is commercial: public bodies must give priority to assessed products, and MSIT may subsidize SMEs' assessments. The decree specifies what the assessment covers and allows it to be done in-house or by a third party; since 21 July 2026 it must also reflect AI-vulnerable groups.
term:Best-Efforts Impact Assessment (Kor.exam_tip: Contrast the EU's FRIA under Art. 27, which is mandatory but applies only to certain deployers.

term:High-Performance AI (Korea).deep_dive: This is not a statutory label but the common name for systems caught by Art. 32. They are systems trained with at least 10^26 FLOPs that also use state-of-the-art technology and pose wide-ranging, significant risks. Their operators must identify, assess and mitigate risks across the lifecycle, run a system to monitor and respond to safety incidents, and submit the results to MSIT. Korea has no separate GPAI tier with documentation or copyright duties.
term:High-Performance AI (Korea).exam_tip: Korea's bar, 10^26 FLOPs plus two qualitative tests, is higher than the EU's 10^25 FLOP presumption of systemic risk.

t_us_ai.overview: The US has no horizontal AI statute. Private-sector organizations instead face a patchwork of state and local laws. Decision laws cover Colorado's ADMT Act, California's CPPA ADMT rules, NYC Local Law 144 and Illinois HB 3773. Frontier-model safety laws are California SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315. Transparency and content laws include Utah's, California SB 942 and AB 2013, and the California and Colorado chatbot laws. Illinois BIPA covers biometrics, and Texas TRAIGA bans intentional misuse. Federally, the TAKE IT DOWN Act targets intimate deepfakes, while EO 14365 and a DOJ task force push back on state laws without preempting them.
t_us_ai.exam: This is new in BOK v2.1 Domain II. Expect scenario questions that turn on one distinguishing detail: which state's law applies, whether the standard is intent (Texas) or effect (Illinois), who enforces, and whether individuals can sue (among these laws, only BIPA and California SB 243 allow it). The numbers matter too: 10 business days' notice and yearly audits in NYC, 30-day explanations and a 60-day cure in Colorado, 15 days versus 72 hours for frontier incidents, and 48-hour takedowns. The biggest currency trap is Colorado: SB 24-205 never took effect.
key_points: Colorado SB 24-205 was repealed before taking effect. SB 26-189 governs consequential decisions from 1 Jan 2027 through notice, a 30-day adverse-outcome explanation, data correction and human review, enforced only by the AG with a 60-day cure
Texas TRAIGA (1 Jan 2026) bans intentional AI misuse. Disparate impact alone is not discrimination, most disclosure duties fall on government, and the AG enforces alone with a 60-day cure

Illinois HB 3773 applies an effect standard to employer AI and bans zip-code proxies. The Video Interview Act requires notice, explanation and consent; BIPA gives individuals a private right of action

The frontier trio (California SB 53, New York RAISE, Illinois SB 315) share the 10^26-operation and $500M-revenue thresholds. Incident deadlines are 15 days in California and 72 hours in New York and Illinois; only Illinois requires annual third-party audits, from 2028

NYC Local Law 144 requires an independent bias audit within the year before use, a public summary and 10 business days' notice. The audit reports impact ratios by sex and race/ethnicity, with no pass/fail threshold
California's stack: AB 2013 training-data summaries, SB 942 provenance (operative 2 Aug 2026), the CPPA ADMT rules (compliance 1 Jan 2027) and SB 243 for companion chatbots (private right of action)
Federal: the TAKE IT DOWN Act requires 48-hour removal, with FTC enforcement from 19 May 2026. EO 14365 cannot preempt state law by itself, and no federal moratorium has been enacted

term:Colorado ADMT Act (SB 26-189).deep_dive: Colorado rewrote its AI law before it ever applied. SB 26-189 dropped SB 24-205's risk-management model (impact assessments, a duty of reasonable care) for a disclosure-and-rights model: notice before use, an explanation of adverse outcomes within 30 days, correction of inaccurate data and meaningful human review, with developers supplying documentation to deployers. HIPAA entities (except for hiring), FDA-regulated devices and compliant insurers are largely carved out.
term:Colorado ADMT Act (SB 26-189).exam_tip: If an answer mentions Colorado impact assessments or a duty of reasonable care, it describes the repealed SB 24-205, not the law that applies from 2027.

term:Texas Responsible AI Governance Act.deep_dive: TRAIGA is a conduct-ban statute rather than a governance mandate: it prohibits AI built or used with intent to cause specific harms and leaves most transparency duties to government agencies. The AG must give 60 days to cure, and a company is not liable if it found the problem through red-teaming, feedback or an internal review while substantially following the NIST AI RMF Generative AI Profile. It also preempts local AI ordinances.
term:Texas Responsible AI Governance Act.exam_tip: TRAIGA requires intent to discriminate and says disparate impact alone is not enough, the opposite of Illinois HB 3773's effect standard.

term:Utah AI Policy Act.deep_dive: Utah paired light disclosure rules with an innovation office and a learning lab that can agree regulatory mitigation with participants. The 2025 amendments narrowed disclosure: ordinary suppliers disclose only on a clear and unambiguous request, while licensed or certified professionals disclose first in high-risk interactions involving sensitive health, financial or biometric data or personalised advice. Blaming the AI is never a defence.
term:Utah AI Policy Act.exam_tip: Utah means disclose when asked, but disclose first in high-risk interactions by licensed professionals.

term:California TFAIA (SB 53).deep_dive: SB 53 is a transparency law for the largest model developers, not a licensing regime. It requires published frameworks and transparency reports, confidential internal-use risk summaries and incident reports to the Office of Emergency Services, and whistleblower protections, all backed by AG penalties. It requires no third-party audits. New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315 copied its thresholds and definitions.
term:California TFAIA (SB 53).exam_tip: SB 53 incidents go to Cal OES within 15 days (24 hours if imminent), compared with 72 hours in New York and Illinois.

term:Large Frontier Developer.deep_dive: The two-part test of frontier compute plus revenue puts the heaviest obligations on a handful of well-resourced companies, while other frontier developers carry lighter transparency and incident-reporting duties. Revenue is counted with affiliates for the preceding calendar year. The same definition appears in all three state frontier laws, so it is a reliable anchor across jurisdictions.
term:Large Frontier Developer.exam_tip: Both limbs must be met: more than 10^26 training operations and more than $500 million in prior-year revenue.

term:California AI Transparency Act (SB.deep_dive: SB 942 tackles synthetic-media deception through provenance. Covered providers must make their AI content detectable (a free detection tool) and traceable (latent metadata naming the provider, system version, time and a unique ID), while visible labels are left to user choice. AB 853 delayed the start to 2 Aug 2026 and extended provenance duties to large online platforms (2027) and makers of cameras and phones (2028).
term:California AI Transparency Act (SB.exam_tip: Latent disclosure is mandatory, the visible (manifest) label is a user option, and text output is not covered.

term:CCPA ADMT Regulations.deep_dive: The CPPA rules turn CCPA rights into AI-specific ones: a specific pre-use notice, an opt-out (unless the business offers a qualifying human appeal or another exception applies) and an explanation of logic and outcome on request. A tool that only supports a human who genuinely reviews the output and can change the decision falls outside the ADMT definition. The same package adds risk assessments and annual cybersecurity audits phased in by revenue.
term:CCPA ADMT Regulations.exam_tip: Know the dates: regulations effective 1 Jan 2026, ADMT compliance 1 Jan 2027, first risk-assessment attestations 1 Apr 2028.

term:NYC Local Law 144.deep_dive: Local Law 144 is a transparency statute: it forces audits, publication and advance notice but does not ban biased tools or set a fairness threshold. It covers tools that substantially assist or replace discretionary hiring or promotion decisions, which DCWP's rules define narrowly. A December 2025 audit by the state Comptroller found the city's enforcement ineffective.
term:NYC Local Law 144.exam_tip: There are three pre-use conditions: an audit within the past year, a public summary, and 10 business days' notice.

term:Bias Audit (NYC LL 144).deep_dive: Under DCWP's rules the auditor must be independent of both the employer and the vendor. The audit uses historical data unless there is too little, in which case test data may be used. It reports rates and impact ratios, plus how many people fell into unknown categories, and may leave out categories under 2% of the data. An employer may rely on a vendor's multi-employer audit only in limited circumstances.
term:Bias Audit (NYC LL 144).exam_tip: An impact ratio below 0.80 does not by itself violate Local Law 144; the law requires calculation and publication, not a passing score.

term:RAISE Act.deep_dive: New York's frontier-model law was substantially rewritten before taking effect: the 2026 chapter amendment repealed the December 2025 text and re-enacted it to track California's SB 53 more closely. It keeps New York-specific features: a dedicated oversight office in the Department of Financial Services, disclosure statements with cost assessments, a 72-hour incident deadline and higher penalties for repeat violations.
term:RAISE Act.exam_tip: RAISE is 72 hours to the DFS office and $1M/$3M; SB 53 is 15 days to Cal OES and $1M.

term:Illinois HB 3773.deep_dive: HB 3773 folds AI into existing civil rights law rather than creating a separate AI regime. Discrimination by an AI tool is the employer's civil rights violation even without intent, and the Act names zip codes as a forbidden proxy. Employers must also give notice of AI use, with the details left to rules from the Department of Human Rights. It sits alongside Illinois's AI Video Interview Act and BIPA.
term:Illinois HB 3773.exam_tip: The test is effect, not intent: an unintended disparate impact from an employer's AI can violate HB 3773.

term:TAKE IT DOWN Act.deep_dive: The Act pairs criminal liability for people who publish nonconsensual intimate images, real or AI-made, with a civil notice-and-takedown duty for platforms. Platforms must remove reported images within 48 hours and make reasonable efforts to remove identical copies. Failures are treated as violations of an FTC rule, and the Act extends that enforcement to nonprofits, which the FTC normally cannot reach.
term:TAKE IT DOWN Act.exam_tip: Remember 48 hours, FTC enforcement from 19 May 2026, and that AI digital forgeries count.

term:Text and Data Mining Exception.deep_dive: Article 2(2) of the DSM Directive defines text and data mining as any automated technique that analyses digital text and data to generate information such as patterns, trends and correlations. The two exceptions differ in who benefits and whether rightsholders can refuse: Article 3 cannot be overridden by contract (Article 7(1)) or by an opt-out, while Article 4 yields to an express reservation. The AI Act ties GPAI providers to the Article 4(3) reservation through Article 53(1)(c), and the Munich Regional Court read the exception as covering corpus-building but not memorisation inside a model (GEMA v. OpenAI, 2025).
term:Text and Data Mining Exception.exam_tip: Commercial trainer: Article 4 plus respect for opt-outs; research organisation doing scientific research: Article 3, no opt-out.

term:Machine-Readable Opt-Out (TDM).deep_dive: Recital 18 of the DSM Directive says that for online content a reservation is appropriate only by machine-readable means, including metadata and the terms and conditions of a website or service; offline, contracts or unilateral declarations can work. The GPAI Code of Practice commits signatories to respect robots.txt and other appropriate machine-readable protocols, and the Commission consulted from 1 December 2025 to 23 January 2026 on which protocols should count as generally agreed. A reservation has no effect on the Article 3 research exception.
term:Machine-Readable Opt-Out (TDM).exam_tip: An opt-out blocks Article 4 mining only; it never blocks Article 3 scientific research by research organisations.

term:Human Authorship Requirement.deep_dive: The D.C. Circuit read the Copyright Act of 1976 as requiring a human author and did not need to decide whether the Constitution also requires one. It stressed that the rule does not bar protection for work made with the assistance of AI; it only denies authorship to the machine itself. The Copyright Office's Part 2 report draws the same line: human-authored material perceptible in an output, or creative arrangement or modification of outputs, can be protected, while expressive elements determined by the machine cannot.
term:Human Authorship Requirement.exam_tip: No human author means no copyright; a human who selects, arranges or edits AI output owns only that human contribution.

term:Fair Use (AI Training).deep_dive: Factor one (purpose, including transformativeness) and factor four (market effect) dominate the AI cases. Bartz called training exceedingly transformative but refused to excuse a central library built from pirated books; Kadrey ruled for Meta only because the plaintiffs offered no evidence of market dilution; Ross rejected fair use where the copying served a direct competitor. The Copyright Office's Part 3 report (May 2025) adds that commercial use of vast troves of works to produce competing content, especially through illegal access, goes beyond established fair use.
term:Fair Use (AI Training).exam_tip: Fair use is a US defence decided case by case; the EU counterpart is the Article 4 TDM exception with opt-outs, not fair use.

term:Product Liability Directive (EU) 20.deep_dive: Adopted on 23 October 2024 and in force since 8 December 2024, the Directive is maximum harmonisation (Article 3). Defectiveness now takes account of a product's ability to keep learning, cybersecurity requirements and the moment it leaves the manufacturer's control (Article 7), and defects caused by software updates, or missing updates needed for safety, within the manufacturer's control cannot be excused as arising after sale (Article 11(2)). Claims expire after 10 years, or 25 years for latent personal injury, and anyone who substantially modifies a product outside the manufacturer's control becomes its manufacturer.
term:Product Liability Directive (EU) 20.exam_tip: PLD means no-fault liability, software counts as a product, and presumptions help claimants; the fault-based AI Liability Directive was withdrawn.

term:AI Liability Directive (Withdrawn).deep_dive: The proposal was the fault-based companion to the no-fault Product Liability Directive, which the Commission proposed the same day and which was adopted in 2024. Work on it was suspended until the AI Act was adopted, the Commission listed it for withdrawal in its February 2025 work programme, and the Parliament's internal market committee called it premature and unnecessary in May 2025. Some of its ideas live on in the revised PLD, which has its own disclosure and presumption rules for no-fault claims.
term:AI Liability Directive (Withdrawn).exam_tip: Any answer that relies on an EU AI Liability Directive presumption is wrong as of 2026: the proposal was withdrawn in October 2025.

term:Executive Order 14281.deep_dive: Section 4 tells agencies to deprioritise enforcement of statutes and regulations to the extent they include disparate-impact liability, naming Title VII's 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2; section 6 orders a review of pending disparate-impact matters; section 5 starts repeal of disparate-impact provisions in Title VI regulations. Agencies followed with concrete steps: the CFPB removed the effects test from Regulation B (effective 21 July 2026) and HUD proposed deleting its discriminatory-effects rule (January 2026). Testing AI for disparate impact remains prudent because courts, states and private plaintiffs are not bound by the order.
term:Executive Order 14281.exam_tip: An executive order changes enforcement priorities, not statutes: Title VII disparate impact still binds employers using AI tools.

term:Adverse Action Notice (ECOA/Reg B).deep_dive: The official commentary requires the stated reasons to relate to and accurately describe the factors actually considered or scored, and notes that more than four reasons is unlikely to help the applicant. The withdrawn Circulars 2022-03 (complex algorithms) and 2023-03 (use of sample forms) applied that rule to AI, and their withdrawal removed guidance but not the regulation. FCRA adds a separate notice under 15 U.S.C. 1681m when information in a consumer report, including any credit score used, contributes to the decision.
term:Adverse Action Notice (ECOA/Reg B).exam_tip: Withdrawn guidance does not withdraw the rule: AI-driven credit denials still need specific, accurate principal reasons.

term:Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation 2.deep_dive: Proposed on 19 November 2025 and politically agreed on 7 May 2026, it was signed on 8 July, published on 24 July and in force from 27 July 2026. The final text sets fixed new high-risk dates rather than a standards-linked trigger. Beyond dates, it replaces Article 4 (AI literacy), adds Article 4a and two Article 5 bans, and gives the AI Office exclusive competence over AI built on a provider's own GPAI model and over AI in very large online platforms. It leaves the risk tiers, penalty ceilings and GPAI obligations untouched.
term:Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation 2.exam_tip: The BOK predates it, so watch the anchor: 'as enacted' puts Annex III high-risk on 2 Aug 2026, 'as amended' on 2 Dec 2027.

term:AI Act Milestone — December 2, 2027.deep_dive: Article 113(c)(i), as replaced by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, starts Chapter III, Sections 1–3 for Article 6(2)/Annex III systems on 2 December 2027. That brings in the whole provider chain (risk management, data governance, documentation, QMS, conformity assessment, registration), deployer duties under Article 26 and FRIAs under Article 27. Systems already on the market before then are caught only after a significant design change, though those intended for public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030.
term:AI Act Milestone — December 2, 2027.exam_tip: Annex III (stand-alone) = Dec 2027 and Annex I (in products) = Aug 2028; any answer giving Aug 2026 for high-risk rules is the pre-Omnibus text.

term:AI Act Milestone — August 2, 2028.deep_dive: Article 113(c)(ii), as amended, applies the high-risk rules on 2 August 2028 to systems that are high-risk under Article 6(1): safety components of, or products covered by, Annex I harmonisation law that need third-party conformity assessment. The Omnibus also moved machinery to Annex I Section B, where AI requirements arrive through sectoral delegated acts applying by the same date. It replaces the original Annex I date of 2 August 2027.
term:AI Act Milestone — August 2, 2028.exam_tip: Product-embedded AI still comes last: 2 Aug 2027 as enacted, 2 Aug 2028 as amended.

term:Code of Practice on Marking and Lab.deep_dive: Drawn up by independent experts in two working groups that mirror Article 50 (providers and deployers), it was published in final form on 10 June 2026, ahead of Article 50 applying on 2 August 2026. Signatories can rely on its measures to show compliance with Article 50(2), (4) and (5); non-signatories must prove their own measures adequate to each market surveillance authority. About 190 organisations had signed by the end of July 2026, and the EU offers icons for labels.
term:Code of Practice on Marking and Lab.exam_tip: Two different codes: the GPAI Code covers Articles 53 and 55 (models); the Marking and Labelling Code covers Article 50 (outputs).

term:Nudification and CSAM Prohibitions.deep_dive: The Commission's May 2026 Article 112 review flagged a gap: generators of non-consensual intimate imagery and of child sexual abuse material were not prohibited. The Omnibus closed it by adding Article 5(1)(ba) and (bb), with scoping rules in Article 5(1a)–(1b). Providers are caught where that output is the intended purpose, or a reasonably foreseeable, reproducible outcome that the system lacks reasonable safeguards to prevent; deployers are caught when they use a system for that purpose.
term:Nudification and CSAM Prohibitions.exam_tip: Eight prohibitions as enacted, ten as amended, and the two new ones start on 2 Dec 2026, not Feb 2025.

term:EDPB Opinion 28/2024.deep_dive: Issued under Article 64(2) at the Irish supervisory authority's request, it answers four questions on AI models. On anonymity, the test is two-sided: extraction from the model and personal data surfacing in answers to queries must both be insignificantly likely. On legitimate interest, it applies the classic three steps, stressing reasonable expectations and mitigations beyond legal minimums. On unlawful training, it sets out three scenarios; a later deployer must check the model's lawful origin unless it was genuinely anonymised.
term:EDPB Opinion 28/2024.exam_tip: No hierarchy of legal bases and no automatic anonymity: 'model weights aren't personal data' is the trap answer.

term:EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 on Web Scra.deep_dive: Building on Opinion 28/2024, the draft applies the GDPR to scraping by private entities for generative-AI training. It stresses purpose limitation, transparency (with the disproportionate-effort route where it applies), minimisation filters, and accuracy checks such as timestamps and validation. For sensitive data it requires an Article 9(2) exception on top of an Article 6 basis, and it suggests GC and Others (C-136/17) may cover incidental collection. It remains a consultation draft until 30 October 2026.
term:EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 on Web Scra.exam_tip: Two locks for sensitive scraped data (Article 6 plus Article 9(2)); 'it was public' is never a blanket exemption.

term:SCHUFA Ruling (C-634/21).deep_dive: A German court referred the case of SCHUFA, whose probability scores lenders relied on. The CJEU held that the score itself can be the Article 22 decision when the lender draws strongly on it, closing a gap in which bureau and lender could each disclaim responsibility. The bureau then needs an Article 22(2) exception and must provide the safeguards and the access information. In AI supply chains, any model output that effectively decides for the customer should be analysed the same way.
term:SCHUFA Ruling (C-634/21).exam_tip: 'Solely automated' can sit upstream: the score-maker, not only the lender, can be the Article 22 decision-maker.

term:Dun & Bradstreet Austria Ruling (C-.deep_dive: A mobile operator refused a €10-a-month contract on the strength of Dun & Bradstreet Austria's credit assessment. The CJEU held that the controller must explain the procedure and principles actually applied, so that the person can see which data were used and how. Neither a complex formula nor a step-by-step technical description is enough, but showing how a change in the data would have changed the result may be. Trade secrets go to the supervisory authority or court for case-by-case balancing, and blanket national exclusions are precluded.
term:Dun & Bradstreet Austria Ruling (C-.exam_tip: Explain the logic actually applied: neither 'here is our algorithm' nor 'it's a trade secret, so no' is a lawful answer.

term:ISO/IEC 42005.deep_dive: The how-to for AI system impact assessment. Clause 5 sets up the organizational process (documentation, integration, timing, scope, responsibilities, thresholds, performing, analysing, recording, approval, monitoring and review); Clause 6 lists what each assessment records (system, data, model, deployment environment, interested parties, benefits and harms, measures). Five informative annexes link it to 42001 (A) and 23894 (B) and supply a harms and benefits taxonomy (C), alignment with other assessments (D) and a template (E).
term:ISO/IEC 42005.exam_tip: Guidance, not certifiable, and for developers, providers and users alike: any option offering a '42005 certificate' or limiting it to developers is wrong.

term:AI System Impact Assessment (ISO/IE.deep_dive: The outward-looking assessment: how could this system, and its foreseeable uses, affect people and society for better or worse? ISO/IEC 42001 makes it mandatory (plan the process in 6.1.4, perform it in 8.4, with Annex A objective A.5), and ISO/IEC 42005 explains how. It records benefits as well as harms, covers failures and reasonably foreseeable misuse, and feeds the organization's risk management rather than replacing it.
term:AI System Impact Assessment (ISO/IE.exam_tip: Impacts on people means 42005; risk to the organization means 23894; the certifiable requirement to do it sits in 42001.

term:Impact Reassessment Trigger.deep_dive: An impact assessment is a living record. Sources on ISO/IEC 42005 agree that a change of intended use or purpose, a significant change to the system itself (new data types, retraining, a replaced model) or a new legal or policy requirement should prompt a fresh look, alongside routine monitoring and review. ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.4 adds assessments at planned intervals or when significant changes are proposed.
term:Impact Reassessment Trigger.exam_tip: In scenario questions, the trigger is the event that changes who is affected or how the system behaves, not administrative events like contract renewals or code moves.

term:ISO/IEC 42006.deep_dive: Published 7 July 2025, ISO/IEC 42006 supplements ISO/IEC 17021-1 with AI-specific requirements for certification bodies that audit AI management systems against ISO/IEC 42001. Accreditation bodies use it to judge whether a certifier is competent and consistent. It is not named in the AIGP blueprint, but it makes a handy distractor.
term:ISO/IEC 42006.exam_tip: 42001 = what you get certified to; 42005 = impact assessment guidance; 42006 = rules for whoever issues the 42001 certificate.

term:OECD Framework for the Classificati.deep_dive: Published in February 2022 (Digital Economy Papers No. 323), the framework helps policy makers characterize an AI system in context. Its five dimensions each carry criteria: People & Planet (users, stakeholders, optionality, rights, well-being), Economic Context (sector, function, criticality, scale), Data & Input (collection, provenance, rights and identifiability, quality), AI Model (type, how built, how used) and Task & Output (tasks, action autonomy, application area). Before deployment ('in the lab') three dimensions apply; after deployment ('in the field') all five do.
term:OECD Framework for the Classificati.exam_tip: Expect 'which dimension holds this criterion?' questions: action autonomy is Task & Output, opt-out and redress are People & Planet, criticality and scale are Economic Context.

term:OECD AI System Definition (2023 Upd.deep_dive: Adopted by the OECD Council on 8 November 2023, the update made five edits: objectives may be explicit or implicit; the system infers from its input how to generate outputs; 'content' joins the outputs, covering generative AI; 'physical' replaces 'real'; and systems may adapt after deployment. The EU AI Act's Art. 3(1) definition closely tracks the new wording, and an explanatory memorandum followed in March 2024.
term:OECD AI System Definition (2023 Upd.exam_tip: Match each edit to its purpose: content means generative AI, implicit objectives means learned goals, physical is a wording clarification.

term:AI Incident vs. AI Hazard (OECD Def.deep_dive: The OECD's May 2024 definitions separate realized from potential harm. An incident is an event where an AI system's development, use or malfunction leads to harm; a hazard is one that could plausibly lead to an incident, and near misses count as hazards. The tiers nest: serious incidents involve serious harm, and AI disasters are serious incidents that overwhelm a community's capacity to cope.
term:AI Incident vs. AI Hazard (OECD Def.exam_tip: Did harm happen? Incident. Could it plausibly have happened, including an error caught in time? Hazard.

term:Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Fram.deep_dive: The G7's Hiroshima Process produced an International Code of Conduct for Organisations Developing Advanced AI Systems (Japan's 2023 presidency). Since February 2025 the OECD has hosted a voluntary, common-format reporting framework so organizations can show how they align with it. The first round produced 25 reports, and version 2.0 opens participation to organizations that deploy and provide advanced AI.
term:Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Fram.exam_tip: The G7 wrote the Code; the OECD runs the reporting; it is voluntary transparency, not certification or legal compliance.

term:OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monit.deep_dive: AIM is the OECD.AI tracker of AI incidents and hazards, built from global news reporting that is automatically classified against the OECD's definitions. It gives policy makers evidence about where AI harms are appearing, but it sees only publicly reported events. The OECD's February 2025 common reporting framework for AI incidents is meant to support more consistent reporting across jurisdictions.
term:OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monit.exam_tip: AIM is compiled from media reports, so it is not a channel for organizations to file their own risk reports; that role belongs to the Hiroshima reporting framework.

ref_42005.overview: ISO/IEC 42005:2025 (published 28 May 2025) is the ISO/IEC guidance standard for AI system impact assessment, and one of the three core ISO standards named in BOK v2.1 II.D. Clause 5 sets out how an organization builds the process: documentation, integration with other management processes, timing, scope, responsibilities, thresholds for sensitive and restricted uses, performing, analysing, recording and reporting, approval, and monitoring and review. Clause 6 sets out what each assessment records: system information, data and data quality, algorithms and models, deployment environment, interested parties, actual and reasonably foreseeable benefits and harms (including failures and misuse), and measures. Five informative annexes link it to ISO/IEC 42001 (A) and 23894 (B) and supply a harms and benefits taxonomy (C), alignment with other assessments (D) and a template (E).
ref_42005.exam: Distinguish it from its neighbours: 42001 is the certifiable management system that requires impact assessment (6.1.4, 8.4, Annex A objective A.5); 23894 covers risk to the organization; 42006 covers the bodies that certify 42001; 42005 is non-certifiable guidance on assessing impacts on people. Expect scenarios on who may use it (developers, providers and users), what belongs in the record, when to reassess, and why it cannot stand in for a GDPR DPIA or an AI Act Art. 27 FRIA.
key_points: Guidance, not certifiable; for any organization that develops, provides or uses AI, of any size
Focus: benefits and harms for individuals, groups and societies, across the AI system lifecycle
Clause 5 = the organizational process (including thresholds for sensitive and restricted uses and formal approval); Clause 6 = what one assessment records
Assess at design and before deployment, keep under review, and reassess on a change of use, a significant system change or a new legal or policy requirement
Annexes: A with 42001, B with 23894, C harms and benefits taxonomy, D alignment with other assessments, E example template
ISO/IEC 42001 requires AI system impact assessment (clauses 6.1.4 and 8.4; Annex A objective A.5); 42005 explains how to meet that requirement
Feeds, but never replaces, a GDPR Art. 35 DPIA or EU AI Act Art. 27 FRIA; not a harmonised standard, so no presumption of conformity

ref_playbook.overview: NIST's online companion to AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1). For each of the Core's 72 subcategories, spread over 19 categories in Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, it gives voluntary suggested actions, transparency and documentation prompts, AI transparency resources and references, and tags the AI actors and topics involved. The RMF states the outcome to reach; the Playbook suggests how to reach it.
ref_playbook.exam: Expect the Framework-versus-Playbook split, the Playbook's voluntary, not-a-checklist, no-certification status, Govern as the cross-cutting function, and scenarios that ask which function or subcategory an activity belongs to, such as MAP 1.1 context-setting, MEASURE 2.x trustworthiness testing, or MANAGE 4.x post-deployment monitoring and incident communication.
key_points: Companion to AI RMF 1.0: one entry per subcategory, with About, Suggested Actions, Transparency and Documentation, and References sections
Voluntary: organizations borrow as many or as few suggestions as fit; it is neither a checklist nor an ordered set of steps, and there is no certification scheme
Govern is cross-cutting and infused throughout Map, Measure and Manage; after Govern, most users start with Map and continue to Measure or Manage
MEASURE 2 (13 subcategories) lines up with the trustworthiness characteristics, from 2.5 valid and reliable to 2.11 fairness and bias
AI Actor tags follow RMF Appendix A: TEVV on every MEASURE subcategory; AI Deployment and Operation and Monitoring on every MANAGE subcategory
Living resource: feedback to AIframework@nist.gov and updates about twice a year; as of 2026 NIST says the next update follows the AI RMF 1.0 revision
Published as web pages plus PDF, CSV, Excel and JSON downloads from airc.nist.gov

term:Suggested Actions (AI RMF Playbook).deep_dive: Each Playbook entry lists suggested actions for its subcategory, from one (MAP 2.1) to two dozen (MEASURE 2.11). They turn an outcome into practical steps: MEASURE 2.11's include identifying types of harm and quantifying them with fairness metrics, and MANAGE 4.1's include red-teaming at a prescribed cadence. NIST says organizations may use as many or as few as apply, and users are not expected to implement them all or in order.
term:Suggested Actions (AI RMF Playbook).exam_tip: An option saying every suggested action must be implemented, or that implementing them earns certification, is wrong.

term:Transparency and Documentation Prom.deep_dive: Under 'Transparency and Documentation', each entry lists questions headed 'Organizations can document the following', then 'AI Transparency Resources', most often GAO-21-519SP, GAO's AI Accountability Framework. The questions help an organization record how it approaches the outcome; MAP 1.5, for instance, asks how the entity identified its maximum allowable risk tolerance. Like the rest of the Playbook they are voluntary.
term:Transparency and Documentation Prom.exam_tip: Suggested actions say what to do; documentation prompts ask what the organization can record and show, and both are voluntary.

term:AI Actors (NIST AI RMF).deep_dive: AI RMF 1.0 borrows the OECD definition, and Appendix A describes each group's tasks. AI Deployment covers piloting, legacy compatibility, regulatory compliance, organizational change and user experience, while TEVV actors test, evaluate, verify and validate throughout the lifecycle and, as a best practice, are kept separate from those who build the models. The Playbook tags each subcategory with the groups most involved, and affected individuals and communities are AI actors even if they never interact with the system.
term:AI Actors (NIST AI RMF).exam_tip: Match tasks to Appendix A: piloting and managing organizational change is AI Deployment, while examining the system and remediating problems is TEVV.

term:AI RMF Subcategory.deep_dive: The Core has four functions, 19 categories and 72 subcategories, numbered by function, category and subcategory, as in MANAGE 1.3. Each states an outcome: MANAGE 1.3 is that responses to high-priority risks are developed, planned and documented, with options of mitigating, transferring, avoiding or accepting. The Playbook has one entry per subcategory, and use-case profiles implement the functions, categories and subcategories for a specific setting.
term:AI RMF Subcategory.exam_tip: A subcategory is an outcome, not a mandatory control: the RMF says organizations may apply some or all of the categories and subcategories.

t_agentic.overview: Agentic architectures are the newest IV.A deployment option: instead of only producing content, an agent plans and takes actions through tools, often over many steps and alongside other agents. Governance shifts from reviewing outputs to bounding what the agent can do (action space) and how freely it decides (autonomy), keeping humans meaningfully accountable, and being able to stop it. Singapore's IMDA Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (v1.5, May 2026) and OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 are the main references; the EU AI Act and GDPR apply through their ordinary definitions.
t_agentic.exam: Expect scenarios: whether a task needs an agent at all (least agency), which control bounds a given risk (least privilege, unique agent identity, sandboxing, system-level approval gates), what to do when oversight decays into rubber-stamping, how to stop a misbehaving agent, and how the AI Act and GDPR Art. 22 attach to an agent's decisions. Traps: prompt instructions offered as sufficient controls, the vendor offered as accountable for the deployer's agent, and dashboard-watching offered as meaningful human involvement.
key_points: Two dials of agent risk: action space (tools and permissions) and autonomy (instructions and human involvement); what an agent can touch drives impact, how freely it decides drives likelihood
Least agency: not every use case needs an agent, and fixed, repeatable processes are better served by deterministic workflows
Bound risk up front: least-privilege, time-bound, non-transferable permissions capped at the authorising human's rights; unique, centrally catalogued agent identities; sandboxes for code execution
Human approval checkpoints for high-stakes, irreversible or atypical actions, enforced at system level, with override rates and review times audited for automation bias
Test whole workflows (tool calls, policy compliance, robustness), agents together as well as alone, and repeatedly; red-team for goal hijack, tool misuse, memory poisoning and cascading failures
Roll out gradually, keep immutable logs, monitor in real time, deny by default when approvals fail, and keep a kill switch that implements the IV.C deactivation policy

Law attaches through general rules: AI Act Art. 3(1) covers varying autonomy, the risk tier follows the use, Art. 25(1)(c) can make a deployer a provider, and GDPR Art. 22 needs meaningful rather than token human involvement

term:Agentic AI.deep_dive: BOK v2.1 names agentic AI alongside generative AI in its scope, and IV.A lists agentic architectures as a deployment option next to fine-tuning and RAG. The IMDA framework notes there is no agreed definition but identifies the common thread: independent planning, decision-making and action over multiple steps toward a user's goal. For governance, errors become actions in the world (a payment made, a file deleted, an email sent) rather than text a person may or may not use.
term:Agentic AI.exam_tip: If the scenario has the system taking actions through tools across several steps, think agentic; if it only produces content for a human to act on, it is generative AI.

term:Action Space (Agentic AI).deep_dive: IMDA separates what an agent can do (action space) from how freely it decides (autonomy). Action space grows with each tool and permission: from a sandbox to internal systems to external APIs, from read to write, or to a computer-use agent that can click and type anywhere. It mainly drives the impact side of risk, which is why least privilege and sandboxing are its main controls.
term:Action Space (Agentic AI).exam_tip: Tools and permissions change action space; instructions and human involvement change autonomy, so expect a question that makes you tell them apart.

term:Tool Misuse.deep_dive: OWASP's ASI02 covers an agent working within its authorised privileges but applying a legitimate tool unsafely, for example deleting records or exfiltrating data after reading a malicious document. It extends the LLM Top 10's Excessive Agency entry to multi-step agent workflows. Mitigations include per-tool least-privilege profiles, sandboxed execution with egress allowlists, a policy gate that checks tool calls before they run, usage budgets and short-lived credentials.
term:Tool Misuse.exam_tip: Misusing privileges it already has is ASI02 Tool Misuse; gaining privileges it should not have is ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse.

term:Agent Goal Hijack.deep_dive: Agents cannot reliably tell instructions from content, so text planted in a web page, email, calendar invite or tool output can reset what the agent is trying to do. OWASP ranks it ASI01, and NIST's January 2025 blog defines agent hijacking as indirect prompt injection that causes unintended, harmful actions. Controls: treat all ingested content as untrusted, lock and version system prompts, require human approval for goal-changing or high-impact actions, and monitor for goal drift.
term:Agent Goal Hijack.exam_tip: Direct, one-off manipulation of goals is ASI01; corruption that persists in stored memory is ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning.

term:Least-Privilege Agent Permissions.deep_dive: The IMDA framework asks that agent authority be scoped, least-privilege by default, time- or session-bound and non-transferable, with explicit escalation for more, and that a human never delegate more access than they hold; delegations should be recorded. OWASP adds just-in-time, short-lived credentials and per-action authorisation for privileged steps. Enforce these limits through access controls at the tool layer, not instructions the model might ignore.
term:Least-Privilege Agent Permissions.exam_tip: An agent's permissions are capped by its authorising human's permissions: delegation can never enlarge access.

term:Human Approval Checkpoint.deep_dive: IMDA lists four triggers: high-stakes actions, irreversible actions (deleting data, sending communications, making payments), outlier behaviour, and user-defined limits. Approval requests should be short and state the risk, and the checkpoint should be enforced by the system rather than a prompt. Because approvers drift into rubber-stamping, IMDA recommends auditing override rates and review times.
term:Human Approval Checkpoint.exam_tip: Irreversibility is the classic trigger: payments, deletions and outgoing messages need a human before the action, not after.

term:Multi-Agent System.deep_dive: Common patterns are sequential (each agent's output feeds the next), supervisor (one agent calls specialists as tools) and swarm (agents work in parallel and hand off). The design lets each agent carry only the tools it needs, but IMDA flags miscoordination, conflicting objectives, collusion and emergent behaviour, and OWASP's ASI07 and ASI08 cover insecure inter-agent messages and cascading failures. Test the agents together as well as individually.
term:Multi-Agent System.exam_tip: Splitting one all-powerful agent into narrow agents improves least privilege but adds interaction risk, and the best answer usually names both.

term:Agent Kill Switch.deep_dive: OWASP recommends kill switches and credential revocation to disable rogue agents instantly, quarantining suspect agents for forensics and requiring fresh attestation and human approval before they return. For supply-chain compromises it suggests revoking specific tools, prompts or connections across every deployment. The switch implements the BOK IV.C deactivation policy; plan the manual fallback too, because staff may have lost the skills to run the process by hand.
term:Agent Kill Switch.exam_tip: The kill switch is the immediate containment step during an incident; the deactivation or retirement policy is the governed decision and process around it.

term:Data Leak.deep_dive: A leak is accidental exposure rather than a deliberate attack: a storage bucket left public, an email to the wrong person, or an employee pasting records into an external AI tool that retains its inputs. Under the GDPR the difference from a hack does not matter, because a personal data breach covers accidental as well as unlawful disclosure or access (Art. 4(12)). The controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk (Art. 33), and must tell affected people without undue delay when the risk is high (Art. 34).
term:Data Leak.exam_tip: Accidental does not mean exempt: a data leak of personal data is a GDPR personal data breach, and the 72-hour clock runs toward the supervisory authority, not toward the individuals.

term:Model Card.deep_dive: Introduced by Mitchell et al. at FAT* 2019, a model card is the model's specification sheet for anyone deciding whether and how to use it: intended and out-of-scope uses, evaluation data and metrics, results broken down by relevant groups and conditions, ethical considerations and caveats. The BOK places creating the model card in release readiness (III.C). It pairs with a datasheet, which documents a dataset, and a system card, which documents how the models and components of a deployed system work together.
term:Model Card.exam_tip: Model card = one model's uses, performance and limits; datasheet = the dataset; system card = the whole deployed system.

term:Fail-Safe Plan.deep_dive: A fail-safe plan answers the question of what happens when the system goes wrong before it is released: it defines the triggers (anomalous outputs, out-of-bounds inputs, lost sensor data), the safe state (halt, fall back to rules, hand over to a person or a backup system) and who may invoke it. The EU AI Act treats backup and fail-safe plans as technical redundancy that supports the robustness of high-risk systems (Art. 15(4)), and Recital 75 describes them as mechanisms that let a system safely interrupt its operation. It complements, rather than replaces, human oversight (Art. 14) and a deactivation policy.
term:Fail-Safe Plan.exam_tip: Fail-safe plans and technical redundancy are tied to robustness in Article 15(4), not to accuracy, cybersecurity or human oversight.

term:Synthetic Data.deep_dive: Synthetic data can come from simulations, rules or generative models trained on real data, and is used to enlarge small datasets, rebalance under-represented groups, test systems, or share data with fewer privacy concerns. It is not automatically anonymous, so re-identification risk still has to be tested. The EU AI Act makes it a first resort for bias work: providers of high-risk systems may process special-category data to detect and correct bias only if synthetic or anonymised data would not do the job (Art. 10(5)(a) as originally enacted; Art. 4a(1)(a) after the 2026 Digital Omnibus).
term:Synthetic Data.exam_tip: Synthetic data mimics real data's statistical patterns; it reduces but does not eliminate privacy risk, and it is the named alternative in the AI Act's bias-detection exception.

term:Reinforcement Learning with Human F.deep_dive: RLHF usually runs in stages: supervised fine-tuning on answers written by people, collection of human rankings of alternative outputs, training a reward model on those rankings, then reinforcement learning to maximize the reward. InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) showed that a 1.3-billion-parameter model tuned this way was preferred by human evaluators over the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. Governance questions include who the raters are, what guidelines they follow, and the risk that the model learns what raters like rather than what is true.
term:Reinforcement Learning with Human F.exam_tip: Human rankings of outputs feeding a reward model point to RLHF; human-written example answers alone point to supervised fine-tuning.

term:Data Poisoning.deep_dive: Poisoning happens before deployment: attackers tamper with the data a model learns from (scraped web content, crowdsourced labels, third-party datasets, fine-tuning data) so it learns wrong patterns or a backdoor that a trigger unlocks later. Because a poisoned model can pass ordinary tests, defences focus on data provenance and integrity controls, vetting of sources, anomaly detection and targeted testing for triggers. NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy (AI 100-2 E2025) treats poisoning and evasion as distinct attack classes, and the EU AI Act lists data poisoning among the AI-specific vulnerabilities in Art. 15(5).
term:Data Poisoning.exam_tip: Poisoning corrupts training data; evasion and prompt injection manipulate inputs at inference time; model inversion and membership inference extract information.

term:Data Quality.deep_dive: Quality is always relative to purpose: the same dataset can suit one use and be unfit for another, which is why the BOK pairs quality with quantity, integrity and fitness for purpose (III.B). Representativeness of the people a system will actually affect deserves particular attention, because gaps there turn directly into biased performance. For high-risk systems Art. 10(3) of the EU AI Act makes these legal criteria, adding that data sets must have appropriate statistical properties for the persons or groups on whom the system will be used.
term:Data Quality.exam_tip: Under-representation of the population a system will serve is a data quality failure under Article 10(3), even if every individual record is accurate.

term:Watermarking.deep_dive: Watermarks can sit in the content itself (pixel, audio or token-level patterns) or in attached metadata, and Recital 133 of the EU AI Act lists them with metadata identifications, cryptographic provenance methods, logging and fingerprints as ways to meet the marking duty. They are imperfect, since editing can weaken or strip them, which is why NIST AI 600-1 suggests measuring the reliability of content-authentication methods such as watermarking. In the AI Act the marking duty sits with the provider of the generating system (Art. 50(2)); disclosing deep fakes is a separate duty on deployers (Art. 50(4)).
term:Watermarking.exam_tip: Providers mark AI output (Art. 50(2)); deployers disclose deep fakes (Art. 50(4)); swapping the two is the classic trap.

term:Automated Decision-Making (ADM).deep_dive: Whether a decision is solely automated turns on the quality of human involvement: the Article 29 Working Party's guidelines (WP251rev.01) say a token sign-off does not count, and a reviewer needs the authority and competence to change the outcome and should consider all the relevant data. Where Art. 22 applies, the decision is allowed only under one of the three exceptions, with safeguards, and it may rest on special-category data only with explicit consent or on substantial-public-interest grounds plus suitable measures (Art. 22(4)). GDPR Recital 71 gives automatic refusal of an online credit application and e-recruiting without human intervention as examples.
term:Automated Decision-Making (ADM).exam_tip: A human rubber stamp does not take a decision outside Article 22; meaningful review requires someone with the authority and competence to change the result.

term:AI Assurance.deep_dive: As in financial audit or product safety, assurance means evidence that a system meets agreed criteria, communicated to the people who need to rely on it. The UK government's Introduction to AI assurance (DSIT, February 2024) describes it as measuring, evaluating and communicating the trustworthiness of AI systems and lists techniques from risk and impact assessment through audits, conformity assessment, formal verification and performance testing to certification. In the BOK it sits with the periodic assessment activities of III.C and IV.C, such as audits, red teaming, threat modeling and security testing.
term:AI Assurance.exam_tip: An audit, a conformity assessment or a red-team exercise is one assurance technique; AI assurance is the program that combines them to build justified trust.

term:Prompt Engineering.deep_dive: Common techniques are clear role and task instructions, system prompts that set rules and refusal behaviour, few-shot examples, output templates and step-by-step instructions. Because it changes no weights and adds no data source it is usually the lightest-weight way to improve a deployed model's fit, but it is also brittle: outputs can shift with small wording changes or model updates, and prompt-level guardrails can be bypassed by prompt injection. BOK IV.A expects candidates to compare using a model as is with fine-tuning, RAG, agentic designs and other ways of improving fit.
term:Prompt Engineering.exam_tip: No weight changes and no external knowledge source means prompt engineering; weight changes mean fine-tuning; documents retrieved at query time mean RAG.
